newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Costello says big four banks can't merge now.
newsitem.headline: Costello says big four banks can't merge now.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Wednesday that the government would end the former government's "Six Pillars" mergers policy, but that at this time mergers between the four major banks would not be allowed.

He said the government would also remove the blanket ban on foreign takeovers of Australian banks, but that the government would apply the principle that any large-scale transfer of Australian ownership of the financial system to foreigners would be contrary to the national interest.

"The government has decided to end the so-called "six pillars" policy, which has involved a blanket ban on any mergers among the major banks and the largest life insurance companies," Costello said in a statement released along with the Wallis Inquiry's report on the Financial System.
"The Treasurer will retain powers to reject mergers under relevant banking and insurance laws," Costello said.
He said he would take into account the assessments of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) when considering mergers.
Australia's major four banks are Westpac Banking Corp, National Australia Bank Ltd, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and the Australian and the New Zealand Banking Group.
The two life offices included in the six pillars policy are the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) and National Mutual Holdings Ltd.
"The government has further decided that mergers among the four major banks will not be permitted at this time," he said.

"This will be reviewed when the government is satisfied that competition from new and established participants in the financial industry, particularly in respect of small business lending, has increased sufficiently to allow such mergers to be considered," he said.
"That goverment has decided to remove the former government's blanket ban on a foreign takeover of any of the major banks," he said.
Any proposed foreign takeover or acquisition would need to be assessed on a case by case basis in accordance with the current Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act, he said.

"In making these assessments, however, the government will apply the principle (as concluded by the inquiry) that any large scale transfer of Australian ownership of the financial system to foreign hands would be contrary to the national interest," he said.
Costello was releasing the government's response to some aspects of the Wallis inquiry into the financial system.
Costello also said the inquiry had made a large number of recommendations to improve the regulatory framework.
"I intend to make a comprehensive statement on financial sector reform later in the year," he said.
He later told a news conference his response would be after the May 13 budget.
